Biblical characters commune with God, expressing their gratitude, distress, and desires. description.en: In Judaism, priests are believed to be the descendants of [Aaron](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/aaron?tab=sources). In the Bible, they are charged with doing the ritual work in the [Mishkan](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/mishkan?tab=sources) and later the Temples, under the leadership of a [high priest](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/high-priest?tab=sources). In Temple times, priests were also entitled to certain gifts and portions of sacrifices. Today, some people of priestly descent recite a special blessing in the synagogue and are careful to avoid contact with corpses, among other responsibilities and restrictions. The Hebrew word for priest is kohen.

description.en: Blessings are declarations of acknowledgement to God about His greatness, His gifts or His connection with the Jewish people via the commandments. While they follow several formats, they all include the key phrase, "Blessed are You, O Lord!"
description.he: הברכות הן הצהרות של הכרה בגדולת האל על מתנותיו ועל הקשר המיוחד שלו עם העם היהודי דרך המצוות. לברכות נוסחים רבים ושונים, אך משותפת להם הפתיחה "ברוך אתה ה', אלוקינו מלך העולם".

description.en: Rabban Gamliel (II) was a tannaitic sage in the first and second centuries CE. He was the first to serve as *nasi* (leader of the *[Sanhedrin](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/sanhedrin?tab=admin)*) after the destruction of the Second Temple and worked to strengthen the Jewish community and leadership in the post-Temple era. Rabban Gamliel occasionally acted in ways that involved publicly shaming other rabbis, which led to pushback and his temporary deposition.
description.he: רבן גמליאל היה בנו של רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. הוא היה נחוש לרכז ולהעצים את כוח הסנהדרין ביבנה כדי למנוע את התפוררות העם היהודי לאחר חורבן בית המקדש, בשאיפה להנחות ולנתב את התסיסה האינטלקטואלית בזמנו. כמה מעמיתיו הבולטים התנגדו למאמציו, והוא אף הושעה מהנשיאות למשך תקופה מסוימת.

description.en: [The Talmud](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Talmud/Bavli) is the textual record of generations of rabbinic debate about law, philosophy, and biblical interpretation, compiled between the 3rd and 8th centuries and structured as commentary on the [Mishnah](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Mishnah) with stories interwoven. The Talmud exists in two versions: the more commonly studied Babylonian Talmud was compiled in present-day Iraq, while the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled in Israel.
